column22:
POSTIVES
 - Clear, scannable product layout on the Home & Property area, and I liked discovering you can split building-only vs contents-only (I didn’t realise that was an option). 
 - Strong “quick actions” design: the left-to-right tiles and obvious paths for make a claim / make a payment / get documents felt practical and “quick and sharp”.
 - Quote journey felt straightforward: I found “get a quote” easy and felt nothin confusing or unexpected in that flow.
 - Key cover info is visible once you’re on the product page (I immediately went to coverage/exclusions and found it useful).
 - Support content had reassuring touches: financial hardship page made me feel more at ease; I liked Quick Exit and the WhatsApp contact option.
 - Live chat performed well: it surfaced the policy document in seconds (and even showed a weather alert), which I rate highly. 

NEGATIVES
 - No obvious search bar was my biggest recurring frustration. I called it a “game changer” for people in a rush and assumed i'd use Google instead.
 - PDS/policy docs felt “hidden” and harder than they should be: I had to click around, deal with small-print links, and I explicitly felt like I was being made to work for it (and questioned the intent).
 - Emergency response info wasn’t prominent: I was surprised it wasn’t front-and-centre, and you said in a real panic I'd already be on the phone by that point.
 - Cookie/banner behaviour created a real UX risk: the emergency banner disappeared after my first visit, so I used incognito and flagged that as something that “needs to be fixed”.
 - Self-serve help without login was “fishing”: for missed payments/FAQs I found the right page partly by accident and said it’d be easier if logged in.

column24:
The PDS PDF itself was informative, but not user-friendly.
 - Helpful/informative: I felt the information was there once I had the document — it spelled out what’s covered and, more importantly for me, what’s not covered (exclusions like wear and tear, defects/poor workmanship, renovations, etc.).
 - Too heavy to “read”: I felt it was big and not something I’d read end-to-end. My approach was OCR and Ctrl+F straight to what I care about (especially exclusions).
 - I relied on tools to interpret it: I felt I’d use ChatGPT/AI to do a gaps/risk analysis and compare PDSs across insurers rather than interpret it manually.
 - Biggest knock wasn’t the PDF - it was access: I felt the PDS link was “hidden” / too hard to locate, which undermines the value of the document because most people won’t persist.
 - Technical side was fine: I felt downloading/opening it worked smoothly (MacBook Pro/Chrome) — no friction there.

What grabbed my attention on the AAMI homepage, immediately:
 - I went straight looking for a search bar — and the fact I couldn’t find one stood out instantly.
 - The top navigation tabs (especially “Home & Property”) grabbed me next because that’s how I orient myself quickly.

 - On my first visit, an emergency banner (Vic fires) caught my eye — and then later I noticed it disappeared (cookie/memory behaviour), which also became a “wait, why is that gone?” moment.
column29:
Yes a few things were genuinely informative:
 - The “what’s covered” vs “what’s not covered” content on the home/contents product pages (I went straight to exclusions like wear and tear, defects/poor workmanship, renovations, etc.).
 - Optional extras I didn’t know existed (e.g., accidental damage at home, free glass cover, and flexible limits), it changed how I think about “who causes the damage” and what can actually be insured.
 - Flood cover detail, I was surprised it’s automatically included/can’t be removed, plus the notes about limits/timing if flood is removed on an existing policy. 
 - Financial hardship information — the page spelled out practical options (payment arrangements, delaying/holding recovery, reduced lump sums, etc.) and the Quick Exit + WhatsApp contact stood out.
 - Missed payment guidance, it was clear my policy “won’t be cancelled right away” and there are steps to keep it active. 
 - Live chat — it surfaced the policy document fast and even flagged a weather alert.
column30:
My experience with “general search” on AAMI:
 - I looked for a search bar immediately and couldn’t find one (I even called it out like “I’ve had my coffee… I’m not missing anything”).
 - Because I couldn’t see an on-site search, I assumed either it doesn’t exist or it’s being avoided to push people to the virtual assistant.
 - So when I needed answers fast (PDS, emergency response, general questions), I defaulted to Google / browser searching and/or live chat instead.

Was it easy to find what I needed?:
 - Not via a site search (because I couldn’t find one). For anything urgent like emergency response, I ended up doing workarounds (including incognito because of banner/cookie behaviour).
 - When I did use an alternate path, chat was fast (policy document in ~15 seconds), and navigation worked when the link was obvious (e.g., Get documents).

How it could be improved (practical fixes):
 - Put a real search bar at the top of the site (persistent across pages) — not buried. I called it a game changer for people in a rush.
 - Make search return direct deep links to high-intent items: PDS / policy documents, certificate of insurance, missed payment, emergency response (bushfire/flood/storm), claims, hardship.
 - Ensure critical info isn’t dependent on cookies/memory (e.g., emergency banner disappearing). If it’s important, it should stay findable every time.
column31:

I also couldn’t see “emergency response” clearly from the homepage and said in a real event I’d be panicking and already on the phone by then.

column42:
1) Add a real, site-wide search (top of every page)
 - A persistent search bar with autocomplete + “best answer” results (PDS, certificates, emergency, missed payment, hardship, claims). I kept looking for this and couldn’t find it.
 - Make results task-led, not marketing-led: “Get PDS (PDF)”, “Get certificate”, “Bushfire hub”, “Pay missed instalment”.

2) Make documents impossible to miss
 - A Documents Centre link in the header/footer and on every product page: PDS / Key Fact Sheet / TMD / example certificate.
 - Stop burying the PDS in small-print links and detours — I called it “hidden” and the pathway didn’t behave how I expected.
 - Add a 1-page plain-English summary (what’s covered / what’s not) before the PDF, because the PDF is long and I’m using OCR + Ctrl+F anyway.

3) Make emergency response unmissable and not cookie-dependent
 - A permanent “In an emergency” button on the homepage + header, with clear entry points: bushfire, flood, storm, evacuation, temporary accommodation.
 - The emergency banner disappearing because of cookies/memory is a genuine UX failure — I had to use incognito to find it again.
 - Add a checklist + what-to-provide + expected wait times right on the hub (that’s what I wanted). 

4) Keep the “quick actions” but make them smarter
 - The tiles (make a claim / make a payment / get documents) are strong — keep them, but add common next steps underneath (certificate, PDS, excess, claim checklist).
- Missed payment should be a one-click fix from the homepage/account area — I had to “go fishing” to land on the right FAQ. 

5) Upgrade chat from “help” to “answer engine”
- Chat was fast and useful (policy doc in ~15 seconds). 
 - Make it even better by: letting me type “PDS” / “certificate” / “bushfire” and getting direct links + the exact doc, plus “speak to a human” when it’s urgent.

6) What would make it genuinely impressive (next level)
 - A Coverage/Gaps Checker: I pick scenarios (“clumsy kid breaks TV”, “flood”, “theft of car keys”), and it instantly shows covered / not covered / optional add-on with the exact reference. That matches how I think (start with exclusions and gaps analysis).
 - I was disappointed there wasn’t an Acknowledgement of Country visible on the website. At minimum: footer + About/Contact, and ideally woven into the brand and community support pages (not tokenistic).
